title: Module 1: IT Fundamentals and Systematic Troubleshooting

spans.caption: A clearly labeled diagram linking a user, computer, operating system, network, and help desk, followed by the six-step troubleshooting loop.

spans.text: IT support helps people use computers, applications, and network services safely and reliably. A good technician does more than remove a fault: they listen, assess impact, explain the work, and record useful details so the issue can be handled consistently if it returns.

Hardware means physical components such as the processor, memory, storage, display, and network adapter. The operating system manages hardware and provides common services; applications help users complete tasks. Power, connectivity, account permissions, and data also affect operation, so a symptom should not automatically be blamed on the computer itself.

Step 1 of the six-step Cisco approach is to identify the problem. Ask what happened, when it began, who and which devices are affected, and what the user was trying to do. Capture the exact error and reproducible steps, recent changes, business impact, and any safety or security concern. Separate observed facts from assumptions.

Step 2 is to establish a testable theory about the likely cause. Rank possibilities from simple to complex: for no sound, check volume and mute state, the selected output device, and then the driver. One symptom can have several causes. Treat a theory as a hypothesis, not a fact, and note the current state before changing anything.

Step 3 is to test the theory with a safe, relevant check. Reproduce the issue if appropriate, inspect status indicators or logs, and change one variable at a time. If the result does not support the theory, record it and consider another cause. Do not run tests that could erase user data or interrupt a service without authorization.

Step 4 is to plan and implement an appropriate solution. Consider expected impact, risk, backups, permissions, and a rollback path; obtain user or change approval when required. Make a controlled change, observe the result, and restore the prior state if it fails. Escalate when the impact or required access exceeds your role.

Step 5 is to verify that the original need—not merely that the computer powers on—has been met. Repeat the user's scenario, check related functions, and make sure the fix did not introduce another issue. Ask the user to confirm. If the result is incomplete, gather the new evidence and return to diagnosis.

Step 6 is to document the work: symptoms, scope, theories considered, tests and results, changes, verification, and outstanding actions. Include useful identifiers such as time, device, and ticket number, but never record passwords or unnecessary personal data. Clear notes let another technician continue and help reveal recurring faults.

Give respectful updates in language the user can understand, avoiding unexplained jargon; say what you will do and when you will follow up. For suspected phishing, malware, a lost device, or a broad outage, preserve relevant evidence, follow organizational procedures, and notify the responsible team promptly. Do not make changes outside your authority.

1 Identify -> 2 Theory -> 3 Test
       ^                  |
       |                  v
6 Document <- 5 Verify <- 4 Plan / Implement
